The biggest issue isn't necessarily the government doing things, it's specifically the Federal government. Lot's of these programs would end up becoming state responsibilities instead, which is more efficient, because states can more accurately fit programs to their needs. Also, moving money away from Washington also removes the incentives for corporations and special interest groups to lobby for national laws -- there is less money and less impact on the state level, and therefor less opportunity to receive nice kickbacks. Others programs/bureaucracies are just way too powerful and intrusive.

Public education: Paul is not opposed to public education on principle; he's opposed to the empirical inefficiencies of the Department of Education. The Department of Education spends about $100 billion every year on making and enforcing arbitrary rules that haven't had any measurable success. Meanwhile, the 90-95% of the money that actually goes straight to the schools is already state and local. The Department of Education is basically a worthless money pit. Paul wants to let the states take the helm, offering more voucher programs and charter schools and generally improving their own affairs.

EPA: Paul isn't against environmental regulations. He's against the EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers constantly making new rules with little oversight and for violating civil liberties. Concerning new rules, he has recently been critical of the proposed changes to the Clean Waterways Act rules, which he has responded to with his own bill to define waterways that you can learn about here: http://www.paul.senate.gov/news/press/sen-rand-paul-introduces-defense-of-environment-and-property-act-of-2015. Concerning civil liberties, he made a big deal out of this case where a family was building a home and the EPA told them they had to stop. The family appealed the decision, and the EPA denied the ability to repeal. Then the family went to the courts, who also refused to allow any kind of an appeals process, which means that the EPA can basically do whatever it wants without repercussions. Meanwhile, the EPA's fines accrued by another $75,000 each day, including the time the family waited for a response from the EPA itself. He doesn't want to get rid of the EPA, but he does want to reign in its powers.

NASA: The Pluto pictures are from the New Horizons program that was first created in 1990, only to get cancelled in 2000. A team from that old program was able to finagle enough funding to get the Pluto flyby mission, which launched in 2006. Today, NASA mostly concerns itself with climate change. Meanwhile, the space exploration industry is starting to privatize, i.e. SpaceX. Paul doesn't want to get rid of NASA, but he does want to cut it's budget to reflect it's changing role.

FCC: Regulating radio waves is one thing; regulating everything else, including the internet, is another matter altogether. He hasn't said he wants to abolish the FCC, but he does want to reduce its regulatory power, especially regarding Net Neutrality. I used to be in favor of Net Neutrality, but now I'm not. At first it sounded like a good idea. It would prevent companies like Comcast from squeezing out small businesses who couldn't or wouldn't pay fees for more bandwidth. What we are forgetting is that Netflix basically started the Net Neutrality movement, because they didn't want to pay more money to ISP's for eating up all their bandwidth (and because their service was really shitty for a while, if you subscribe and remember that period). With Net Neutrality, there is less incentive for other businesses to compete with the established ISP's. There are less areas of the market to compete on. Now instead of being able to negotiate better contracts with the ISP's, you're stuck paying whatever their blanket rates would be. Without that ability to negotiate, there isn't much of a reason for other ISP's to enter the market. Fixed costs are already high, but throw in the fact that you would have to cut prices across the board when dealing with individual companies in order to beat out a company like Comcast and suddenly entering the market is a serious chore. There isn't any room for niche providers who would focus on offices, or homes, or apartments, etc. Net Neutrality is well-intentioned, but it's just going to help perpetuate the oligopolies. So regarding Paul again, he doesn't want to abolish the FCC, just reign in it's powers in order to foster competition.

ACA: I don't know how anybody could like this law, unless you sell health insurance. I worked in finance a few years in Bermuda. Aside from Switzerland and maybe Delaware, tax havens weren't that popular until the 1960s. It all really started with insurance companies setting up captive offshore insurance companies in Bermuda. These companies could book premium and pay a much lower income tax, sending pre-taxed profits back to their owners, now exempt through a taxation treaty against double-taxation. Now medium-sized businesses and even wealthy individuals are getting in on the act. 90% of Fortune 500 companies have an offshore captive insurance company or one of those other useful entities, holding companies and shell-subsidiaries. Google Ireland, for example, miraculously earns 90% of Google's worldwide revenues. Or let's say you own a 200-hotel chain in the US; you can set up an offshore holding company that (on paper at least) owns the whole shebang and leases the hotels back to you. Boom. Now, you have no profits to tax in America. In fact, financialization, globalization and deregulation have worked together over the past 30 years to cripple tax fairness. This is more than tax loopholes, it's a fundamental tax rift between rich and poor. Hedge fund managers who earn hundreds of millions a year in income pay a 15% tax rate. The horrors that have been done in the name of the One Child Policy are common knowledge, and with this in mind, as well as the troubling demography of China, the Communist Party of China has formally scrapped the One Child Policy and replaced it with a Two Child Policy for all in China.

This is something that the government has been considering, and under Wu Qiang’s administration this has finally come to fruition. Couples are encouraged to have two children, a boy and a girl, for the future of China.

“We have decided that the One Child Policy is no longer useful,” Wu Qiang stated, “The mechanization of our agriculture allows us to support population growth. Indeed, China needs growth. We will set behind us the horrible past of this policy and look forward to a better, brighter future!”

The move has been met with support from the people of China. Some critics, however, say that just because there are now two allowed doesn’t mean that the horrors of the One Child Policy will end. “Now it’ll be the third child, rather than the second,” an anonymous academic told us, “It may be less terrible, but it is still terrible nonetheless”.

With the Two Child Policy the Communist Party hopes to see growth in the Chinese population, and a healthier demography coming from it.
